title: Worry about the unexpected
hook: worry only about what cannot happen; this is the world's way, nothing stays (Salok M9 51, ang 1429)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama gone, Ravana gone, and your line: even they went. Did someone great come to mind? This week ran like a dream and a show, youth has gone, head shakes, the Name carries across, hold it lightly, and Rama gone. Today the ninth Guru turns to worry. Day six hundred two.

It's 2am and the list is running. The car is making a noise. Your father's knees are worse. The kids will leave home one day. You'll get older. So will everyone you love. Some of these are real problems. But look closely at the list and notice something odd: a lot of what keeps us awake is not a surprise at all. It's the most predictable thing in the world. Bodies age. Things wear out. People move on. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a two-line salok about exactly this list, and it has a twist in its first line that makes people stop and read it twice. Today: worry about the unexpected.
screen: `2AM, AND THE LIST IS RUNNING.` → `MOST OF IT IS NO SURPRISE.` → `A SALOK WITH A TWIST.`

segments.voice: The salok is number fifty-one of the fifty-seven near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang fourteen twenty-nine. It opens: chinta taa kee keejeeai, jo anhonee hoi. In paraphrase: worry about the thing that would be anhonee, the thing that cannot happen, the thing nobody expects. Chinta is the everyday Punjabi word for worry, the one a grandmother uses when you're late home. Anhonee is the odd one: the not-happening, the impossible. So the line sounds backwards at first. Worry only about what can't happen? Then the second line explains. Ihu maarag sansaar ko: this is the road of the world. Nanak, thir nahee koi: nothing stays, nobody stands still. Here's the turn. Change is not the anhonee. Change is the most certain thing there is. Aging, loss, the end of a season: these are the road itself. If something truly unexpected came along, maybe that would deserve worry. But the things we dread most are the things the world has always done. Worrying about them is like worrying that the sun will set. Notice what the Guru doesn't say. He doesn't say nothing matters, or that you shouldn't care for your father's knees. Care is one thing; chinta is another. Care takes him to the doctor. Chinta lies awake rehearsing a loss that hasn't come, as if fear could stop the road from being a road. Remember who's speaking. These saloks are traditionally linked to the last part of Guru Tegh Bahadur's life, in the years before his execution in Delhi in 1675. The calm in them isn't the calm of someone with an easy life. It's calm that looked straight at the road.
screen: `CHINTA: WORRY. ANHONEE: WHAT CAN'T HAPPEN.` · `THIS IS THE ROAD OF THE WORLD.` · `CHANGE IS NOT THE SURPRISE.` · `CARE IS ONE THING; WORRY IS ANOTHER.` · then, large: `NOTHING STAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one expected worry. Sit comfortably and let the list come up. Pick one worry that is really about something the world always does: getting older, a child growing up, a season ending. Name it plainly. Then ask: is there one thing I can actually do about this? If there is, note it for later. If there isn't, breathe out and set it down, the way you'd put a heavy bag on the floor. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you let it go. The bell holds the time.
Worry about the unexpected. Chinta for the anhonee: save worry for what can't happen, because change is the road itself.
Your line: nothing stays. The next time a predictable worry comes back today, say the line once and ask what care, not chinta, would do. Day six hundred two.

screen: `DAY 602 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHATEVER IS BORN WILL PASS.`

howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are read near the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and many Sikhs know salok fifty-one by heart as a word against needless worry.

myth: the salok tells people to stop caring about those they love
it separates care, which acts, from chinta, which only rehearses loss.
the salok says change is the most certain thing on the road
aging and loss are the road itself, not the surprise.
this salok is from Guru Nanak's Japji
it's salok fifty-one of Guru Tegh Bahadur's fifty-seven, on Ang 1429.

fork.setup: it's 2am and you're dreading that your parents are getting older. by salok fifty-one, what's the move?
options: do the care you can do, and set the chinta down.
fork.reveal: aging is the road of the world, not the anhonee. the Guru leaves room for care; it's the sleepless rehearsal he questions.

original.note: Gurmukhi: chinta, worry; the everyday Punjabi word, and the first word of salok fifty-one.

trapdoor: what you thought: worry about the unexpected means expect the worst.
what it means: change is certain, so save worry for what can't happen, which is to say, almost nothing.
what a scholar hears: anhonee (the not-happening) is set against the road of the world; the salok sits among the 57 Saloks Mahalla 9 on Angs 1426–1429.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, salok 51 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429)

notes: Transliteration chinta taa kee keejeeai jo anhonee hoi / ihu maarag sansaar ko naanak thir nahee koi: confirm wording and numbering as salok 51.
Reading of anhonee as 'what cannot happen / the unexpected': confirm this is a mainstream reading; some translators render it 'the unexpected'.
The link between the saloks and the last part of the Guru's life (before 1675) is traditional; confirm phrasing.
